Nepal’s power system is transitioning from a predominantly hydro-based electricity system toward a larger, more interconnected and increasingly flexible renewable-energy system. Rapid hydropower development, growing electricity demand, seasonal generation variability, and the emerging integration of solar and other variable renewable energy resources create a growing need for grid-scale energy storage. This paper evaluates the technical and economic role of pumped-storage hydropower (PSH), using a proposed 500 MW pumped-storage project in Nepal as a case-study framework. The study combines storage-duration and efficiency calculations with discounted cash-flow analysis and scenario-based sensitivity testing of capital cost, round-trip efficiency, annual cycling, electricity-price spread, and financing conditions. An illustrative base case assumes an 8-hour storage duration, 75% round-trip efficiency, 300 equivalent full cycles per year, USD 1,200/kW capital cost, a USD 50/MWh charging-to-discharge price spread, 8% discount rate, and 40-year economic life. Under these stated assumptions, the project provides approximately 4,000 MWh of usable discharge energy per cycle and an indicative NPV of about USD 86 million, with an IRR of approximately 9.3% and a simple payback of about 10.4 years. The sensitivity analysis shows that electricity-price spread, annual cycling, capital cost, and financing conditions have the strongest effects on project value. The paper concludes that Nepal should assess PSH as a multi-service flexibility asset rather than through energy-only project appraisal, with capacity and ancillary-service remuneration required to strengthen bankability.

This study numerically investigates the influence of Tip Speed Ratio (TSR) on the performance of a jet-driven four-bladed waterwheel for low-head hydropower applications using transient Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). A two-dimensional transient model was developed in ANSYS Fluent, employing the Shear Stress Transport (SST) k–ω turbulence model to simulate the unsteady interaction between the water jet and the rotating runner. Simulations were conducted for eight operating conditions corresponding to runner speeds of 10–45 rpm at a constant inlet jet velocity of 3.0 m/s. The transient torque histories were analysed to determine the average torque, mechanical power, hydraulic efficiency, power coefficient, and corresponding TSR. The results show that waterwheel performance is strongly influenced by TSR. The highest average torque of 169.48 Nm was obtained at 10 rpm (TSR = 0.244), while the maximum mechanical power of 489.72 W, hydraulic efficiency of 60.57%, and power coefficient of 0.606 occurred at 35 rpm, corresponding to an optimum TSR of 0.855. The transient torque profiles exhibited periodic oscillations due to successive blade–jet interactions. The findings demonstrate that operation near the optimum TSR maximizes energy extraction and provides useful guidance for the design and optimization of jet-driven waterwheels for decentralized low-head hydropower generation.

The Grindulu PS Hydroelectric Power Plant is one of the hydroelectric power plants that relies on the flow of the Grindulu River as its primary energy source. Due to the irregularity of water discharge, particularly at its lowest point during the dry season, the Grindulu PS Hydroelectric Power Plant is planned to be constructed using variable speed drive (VSD) technology [1], [2]. The objective of this study is to analyze the hydrological and hydraulic data of the Grindulu River to determine the annual water discharge profile, particularly during the dry season; to analyze the minimum potential for electricity generation from the Grindulu PS Hydroelectric Power Plant based on the lowest available discharge; and to analyze the Variable Speed Drive (VSD) system of the Grindulu PS Hydroelectric Power Plant in optimizing electricity generation under minimum discharge conditions during the dry season. This study is a quantitative-predictive analysis aimed at modeling inflow predictions at the proposed site for the Grindulu Hydropower Plant, which is planned to utilize a pumped-storage system. The prediction model used is the Bi-Directional Long Short-Term Memory Sequence-to-Sequence (Bi-LSTM Seq2Seq) with a Quantile Regression (QR) approach to generate inflow estimates at various levels of uncertainty (q10, q50, and q90) [3]. The research results show that the flow characteristics of the Grindulu watershed are dominated by relatively constant low-flow conditions throughout the year, particularly during the dry season, as indicated by the q50 and q90 flow values, which are both 1.021 m³/s. This indicates that the flow is dominated by baseflow and that high-flow events occur only for limited periods. With a minimum flow potential and a reservoir system design flow of 242 m³/s, a generation capacity of +1,000 MW can be achieved by utilizing the water stored in the upper reservoir. At the Grindulu River Basin hydroelectric power plant, the VSD system allows for more flexible and efficient operation of the pump-turbines, ensuring that power generation remains normal even under minimum flow conditions. The analysis results indicate that the hydraulic technical parameters that need to be considered in supporting the implementation of the VSD system under minimum flow conditions are water flow, effective head, reservoir water level fluctuations, turbine efficiency, and flow stability [2].

The Sutlej River, a major tributary of the Indus River system, holds significant strategic, economic, and environmental importance for South Asia. Flowing through China (Tibet), India, and Pakistan, the river serves as a vital source of irrigation, hydropower generation, and freshwater supply for millions of people. However, increasing water scarcity, climate change, rapid population growth, and expanding infrastructural developments have intensified the hydro political challenges associated with its management. Although the Indus Waters Treaty (1960) has long been regarded as one of the world's most successful transboundary water-sharing agreements, emerging environmental and geopolitical realities have exposed limitations in its capacity to address contemporary water security concerns. This study explores hydro politics of Sutlej River by looking at the connection between transboundary water governance and regional cooperation in South Asia. The study employs a qualitative case study method, relying on secondary sources, such as official documents on the treaty, government publications, academic literature, and documents by other organizations internationally. Thematic analysis serves to determine the viability of the current governance mechanisms, key environmental and political obstacles of the collaborative water management of India and Pakistan, and the prospects of enhancing the same. The results indicate that despite the fact that the Indus Waters Treaty has helped in avoiding large-scale interstate water wars, the treaty needs institutional adjustment to adapt efficiently to changing climatic circumstances, rising water demands, environmental degradation, and the shifting security landscape in the regions. The study postulates that better water diplomacy, openness in data sharing, integrated river basin management and strong regional institutions are critical to encouraging sustainable water management. Demonstrating the Sutlej River as a resource of strategic significance and a possible site of collaboration, the study will be a part of the further discussion on transboundary water governance and will provide policy initiation to promote regional stability, ecological and long-term water security in South Asia.

The Sub-regional Launching Workshop of the CGIAR Multifunctional Landscapes Science Program (MFL-SP) for the Omo-Ghibe Living Landscape was organized in Wolaita Zone to officially introduce the program and engage key stakeholders in a shared vision for sustainable landscape management and livelihood improvement. The workshop brought together representatives from government institutions, universities, research organizations, development partners, NGOs, community representatives, and the private sector to discuss the major environmental, socio-economic, and governance challenges affecting the Omo-Ghibe basin and identify opportunities for integrated landscape restoration and development. The Omo-Ghibe Living Landscape is a strategically important and ecologically diverse area that supports agriculture, pastoralism, fisheries, hydropower generation, and biodiversity conservation. However, the landscape is increasingly threatened by land degradation, soil erosion, deforestation, declining soil fertility, landslides, climate variability, flooding, and growing pressure on natural resources driven by rapid population growth and unsustainable land-use practices. These challenges have negatively affected agricultural productivity, ecosystem services, and community livelihoods. The workshop emphasized the importance of adopting integrated, science-based, and multi-stakeholder approaches to address these interconnected challenges. The CGIAR Multifunctional Landscapes Science Program was presented as a platform to promote resilient, productive, and inclusive landscapes through coordinated interventions that balance environmental sustainability, livelihood improvement, and economic development. The event also created an opportunity to review past and ongoing restoration efforts, identify priority interventions for target districts, strengthen stakeholder coordination, and align ongoing initiatives under a common landscape management framework. Through keynote speeches, technical presentations, and breakout group discussions, participants highlighted both the critical challenges and the strong opportunities for sustainable transformation in the Omo-Ghibe landscape. The workshop concluded with a shared commitment among stakeholders to strengthen collaboration, enhance evidence-based planning, and support the successful implementation of the MFL-SP in the region.

Jatigede Reservoir is a strategic water resources infrastructure in West Java that supports raw water supply, irrigation, hydropower generation, flood control, fisheries, and socio-economic activities. However, the sustainability of these functions is threatened by erosion in the catchment area, which contributes to reservoir sedimentation. The sedimentation rate is estimated at approximately 7.04 mm year-1 with a volume of ±1.07 million m³, while watershed erosion reaches 5.320 mm year-1. These processes accelerate reservoir siltation and reduce storage capacity, emphasizing the need for effective watershed management. This study applied the Revised Universal Soil Loss Equation (RUSLE) to estimate soil erosion and the Sediment Delivery Ratio (SDR) to predict sediment yield. The analysis utilized soil type maps, Digital Elevation Model (DEM) data, Sentinel satellite imagery, and monthly rainfall data collected over a ten-year period. A literature review was also conducted to develop practical conservation recommendations. The results showed that erosion in the Jatigede Reservoir catchment area was generally low, with an average rate of 16.703 tons ha-1 year-1, and was dominated by very slight to slight erosion classes covering approximately 88.81% of the area. Higher erosion rates were concentrated on steep slopes and areas with limited vegetation cover. The average sediment yield was 3.983 tons ha-1 year-1 (SDR = 0.23), equivalent to approximately 786 thousand m³ year-1. Based on the reservoir's dead storage capacity of 103 million m³, the estimated service life of the reservoir is about 131 years. To reduce erosion and sedimentation, the study recommends the implementation of soil conservation measures to support the long-term sustainability of the reservoir.

The transition toward renewable energy systems increasingly requires solutions that improve energy efficiency while accounting for the coupled interaction between water resources, energy production, and economic performance. This study investigates a grid-interactive hydropower system enhanced with tailrace hydrokinetic energy recovery as a means of improving water resource utilisation without major infrastructure modifications. By recovering residual kinetic energy from hydropower tailraces, the proposed configuration enables a combined-cycle hydropower system that exploits both the potential and kinetic energy of water. The main contribution of this work is the development of an integrated techno-economic optimisation framework that explicitly couples hydropower operation, tailrace hydrokinetic energy recovery, reservoir dynamics, and grid interaction. A site-specific nonlinear relationship between hydropower outflow and tailrace flow velocity is derived from measurements and embedded directly into the optimisation model, allowing hydrokinetic power generation to be represented without simplified assumptions. Reservoir dynamics are further enhanced by incorporating evaporation and precipitation as exogenous variables, enabling the coupled behaviour of water availability, energy dispatch, and economic performance to be evaluated. Open-loop, closed-loop, and model predictive control strategies are formulated and comparatively assessed. Simulation results demonstrate that integrating hydrokinetic turbines into hydropower tailraces can achieve net energy savings of up to 63% and reduce net energy costs by approximately 61%, relative to a baseline grid-interactive hydropower system without hydrokinetic recovery under identical daily operating conditions and load demand. Annual analysis shows comparable trends, with savings remaining above 60% over the full-year horizon. Model predictive control provides the most robust operational performance by effectively aligning generation with demand while maintaining reservoir constraints. Economic analysis indicates that the cumulative operational savings generated by the hydrokinetic integration offset the initial hydrokinetic investment cost after approximately 1.1 years, while the overall discounted payback period is estimated at 2.88 years over the 20-year project horizon. The results confirm that tailrace hydrokinetic energy recovery offers a scalable and economically attractive pathway for improving resource efficiency at the energy–water interface.

Social innovation development is increasingly urgent to address the dynamic socio-ecological challenges in Wonogiri Regency, where environmental degradation and community vulnerabilities intersect. In Pokohkidul Village, these challenges are manifested through reservoir sedimentation, household waste generation, and socio-economic vulnerabilities among communities surrounding the Wonogiri Hydropower Plant. In response, the BENGAWAN SOLO Program (Bangun Ekonomi dan Lingkungan melalui Wawasan Sinergi Potensi Lokal) developed the ARUS-ASIH community empowerment ecosystem to transform environmental burdens into productive assets. The program was implemented through sequential development stages, beginning with environmental and socio- economic diagnosis, followed by solution design and prototyping through a living laboratory, agricultural demonstration plots, and the Women Farmers Group “Lestari.” Program consolidation was strengthened through mechanization of the SEDARU Production House, youth capacity building, and Waste Bank digitalization, while scaling was pursued through the SEDARU Learning Center and regional fertilizer distribution. Systemic change was achieved through governance transfer to a local consortium. By integrating environmental management with livelihood development, the program increased agricultural productivity, created alternative income opportunities, continuously utilized organic and inorganic waste, optimized reservoir sediment utilization, and generated a positive Social Return on Investment (SROI), demonstrating a pathway toward resilient and sustainable community development.

DescriptionLREM — Low-Flow Reservoir Evolution Model is a mathematical and computational framework developed by Marcelo Moncayo Theurer / THEK Research Institute to analyze the evolution of reservoir water levels during low-flow periods and their relationship with hydropower generation constraints and potential electricity rationing.This work presents the 2026 application of LREM to the Mazar Reservoir in Ecuador, integrating the FGET → VRR → NFF methodological framework. The model evaluates reservoir elevation behavior, seasonal low-flow intensity, critical thresholds, and the corresponding potential duration of daily power outages.The study includes both the original calibrated LREM projection and an adjusted 2026 curve based on observed reservoir behavior. The adjusted scenario indicates a substantially less severe condition, with the reservoir remaining above the maximum-risk threshold and with a calculated peak energy deficit equivalent to approximately one hour of daily outage, a level that may be absorbed through energy-management measures without widespread power cuts.The publication is provided in English and Spanish and includes This research proposes an artificial intelligence (AI)-driven dispatching framework for modern power systems integrating conventional power plants, renewable energy sources, and energy storage systems. The increasing penetration of renewable energy introduces significant uncertainty and variability, which challenges traditional economic dispatch methods such as the Merit Order approach. These conventional methods are limited in their ability to handle time-dependent decision-making and to optimally utilize energy storage systems.To address these challenges, this study formulates the economic dispatch problem as a sequential decision-making process and applies a reinforcement learning (RL) approach using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). The proposed framework enables an agent to learn optimal dispatch strategies by interacting with a simulated power system environment that includes generator constraints, renewable generation variability, and battery state-of-charge dynamics.The performance of the proposed method is evaluated through a custom simulation scenario and compared with the conventional Merit Order approach. The results demonstrate that the PPO-based dispatch strategy incurs a modest operational cost premium while improving the utilization of renewable energy and energy storage systems. In addition, the learned policy exhibits the ability to perform temporal optimization, such as charging the battery during periods of excess renewable generation and discharging during peak demand.The study decomposes the dispatch problem into two sub-problems, each solved by the most appropriate method. Generator scheduling is assigned to the Merit Order rule, which is provably optimal for thermal dispatch under standard economic dispatch assumptions. Intertemporal storage arbitrage, charging and discharging a battery energy storage system (BESS) and a pumped storage hydropower (PSH) unit, is delegated to a reinforcement learning agent trained with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO). This hierarchical decomposition reduces the RL action space from six dimensions to two and concentrates all learning capacity on the temporal storage problem that rule-based methods cannot solve.Three strategies were evaluated under identical 24-hour simulation conditions on a Thailand-scale grid calibrated to EGAT operational statistics: deterministic Merit Order, the proposed Hybrid Merit Order–PPO, and fully autonomous PPO. The Merit Order baseline achieves the lowest total operating cost (1,085,936,384 THB/day) but depletes storage reserves before the evening demand peak. The Hybrid PPO agent learns a clear temporal arbitrage strategy, drawing down PSH overnight, recharging during the midday solar window, and discharging at the evening peak , at a marginal cost premium of +1.4%, attributable to storage cycle wear and the fuel-cost shift associated with active storage management. The agent also learns to concentrate on PSH rather than BESS, reflecting the economic advantage of PSH's lower cycle cost. The fully autonomous PPO agent (+9.4%) confirms the value of the decomposition. Without it, the agent must rediscover the Merit Order principle from scratch and does not converge to a cost-competitive policy within the training budget.The results demonstrate that reinforcement learning can acquire temporal reasoning about storage. The inclusion of explicit battery degradation cost is shown to be decisive when evaluating storage dispatch strategies. The proposed hierarchical architecture offers a practical and interpretable path toward RL-assisted dispatch in real power systems.Overall, this study highlights the potential of reinforcement learning as a promising tool for intelligent power system operation and provides a foundation for future development of AI-based dispatch strategies in smart grids.

Renewable-capacity planning in hydro–wind–photovoltaic–pumped-storage hybrid energy systems is jointly affected by wind–photovoltaic output, inflow, renewable capacity, and photovoltaic capacity ratio, yet their coupled effects on operation and capacity preference remain unclear. This study develops a scenario-based resource–operation–capacity evaluation framework for a cascade hydropower–wind–photovoltaic–pumped-storage system. Five cumulative-probability levels of wind–photovoltaic joint output and five hydrological exceedance-frequency levels form 25 combined scenarios. Normalized historical recurrence weights are derived through similar-year intersections from 26 assigned historical years. In each scenario, 210 fixed combinations of renewable capacity and photovoltaic capacity ratio are evaluated using a medium- and short-term operational model solved by the non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II). A two-level decision method identifies the highest-scoring configuration in each scenario and then aggregates configuration scores across all scenarios using recurrence weights. Application to the clean-energy base in the middle reaches of the Yalong River Basin shows that inflow dominates operational-performance variation by affecting hydropower availability and the generation-plan level. Wind–photovoltaic resource conditions alter the balance between renewable output and flexible regulation, whereas the photovoltaic capacity ratio changes joint-output stability and the regulation required from cascade hydropower and pumped storage. Increasing renewable capacity raises transmitted energy, but excessive expansion increases curtailment and load-loss risks. The scenario-dependent highest-scoring configurations span 9000–12000 MW and photovoltaic capacity ratios of 35 %–55 %. Cross-scenario weighting identifies 9000 MW and a 40 % photovoltaic capacity ratio as the probability-weighted optimal configuration under the adopted settings. The framework links representative resource conditions, system operation, and capacity decisions for hydro-dominated renewable-energy planning.

Purpose: This study examines license hoarding in Nepal’s hydropower sector, where over 42,000 MW of potential remains underutilized due to systematic project delays, and quantifies its economic and environmental consequences. Design/methodology/approach: Using a novel project level dataset of 847 hydropower licenses issued between 2000 and 2025, the study integrates real options theory with institutional economics. It employs Probit, Cox proportional hazards, panel fixed effects, and instrumental variables models, complemented by Random Forest with SHAP values, counterfactual generation analysis, and welfare loss estimation. Findings: Weak institutional enforcement is the primary driver of hoarding increasing delay probability by 34.2% when combined with speculative ownership. Macroeconomic uncertainty amplifies the option value of waiting. License hoarding causes annual foregone electricity of 4,287 GWh, economic losses equal to 2.3% of GDP, and excess emissions of 2.8 million tons of CO2e. Policy simulations show that escalating penalties and binding milestones could lower inactivity by 41.3%. Implications: Strengthening enforcement and introducing performance based licensing can accelerate green transitions in developing economies. Originality/value: Relatively little work has been done to systematically quantify institutional inefficiencies in renewable energy licensing. This study contributes to the literature by providing evidence-based pathways for policy reform. JEL Classifications: L51, Q42, Q28, Q48

The article examines directions for ensuring sustainable economic development in Uzbekistan based on green innovation and technological modernisation, using data from the Ministry of Energy and the National Statistics Committee. Solar and wind generation rose from 0.43 billion kWh in 2022 to more than 10.5 billion kWh in 2025, and the share of green generation reached 19.4% of total electricity output. At the same time, an estimated 23% decline in hydropower output highlights climate risks, and reaching the 54% target by 2030 requires green generation to grow by 29–31% annually. Evidence-based recommendations on green finance, energy efficiency, industrial modernisation, research and innovation, and regional development are proposed.

The increasing penetration of converter-interfaced renewable generation in hybrid wind–hydro power systems strengthens the frequency-regulation requirements imposed on hydropower plants, particularly in isolated power systems. In Pelton turbine installations, the deflector, traditionally used as a safety device, has recently been incorporated as an active element for frequency regulation. By rapidly modifying the fraction of the jet reaching the runner without immediately changing the penstock flow, the deflector mitigates the influence of pressure-wave dynamics on the plant response, although its operation entails hydraulic-energy losses due to jet diversion. This study proposes a modal-analysis-based tuning criterion for a coordinated needle–deflector control scheme (CCS) with a proportional-integral controller. In this configuration, the proportional action is assigned to the deflector and the integral action to the needle. The proposed method combines an eigenvalue sensitivity–speed assessment based on modal settling time and eigenvalue sensitivity with characteristic-polynomial coefficient matching to derive closed-form expressions for the controller gains. Root-locus trajectories and modal properties confirm the prescribed eigenvalue structure and demonstrate the advantages of the proposed tuning criterion over the conventional Paynter criterion. The resulting controller is evaluated using a detailed nonlinear elastic model based on one hydraulic branch of the Coca Codo Sinclair Hydropower Plant in Ecuador. Under a sudden increase in demand, the CCS improves the frequency nadir, reduces power oscillations, and accelerates frequency recovery compared with the conventional needle control scheme. Simulations of a hybrid wind–hydro power system under variable wind generation further show that the proposed controller can substantially increase the admissible wind-power penetration while maintaining adequate frequency regulation. For the analyzed scenario, the additional wind energy accommodated by the coordinated scheme exceeds the hydraulic-energy cost associated with jet diversion, indicating a favorable trade-off between frequency regulation performance, renewable-energy integration, and hydraulic losses.

ABSTRACT Southeast Asia's economic growth demands substantial energy investment. This study investigates China's official financing for power generation in the ASEAN region since 2000 through a systematic mapping approach. Findings show that China has primarily supported coal and hydropower projects, especially in Indonesia, Vietnam, and Laos, while offering minimal renewable energy financing. This is mainly attributed to unfavorable local policy environments and China's focus on large‐scale infrastructure. The study also highlights widespread local resistance—particularly to coal projects—driven by environmental and livelihood concerns. The forms of mobilization were shaped by the political freedom in each country. While official Chinese coal financing largely ceased after 2019, aligning with Beijing's international climate commitments, questions remain about the enforcement of this pledge and the broader shift toward green energy. The study concludes by examining the structural and political barriers that have historically favored fossil fuel investments over renewables in the region.

Hydropower remains a major source of affordable, clean, and reliable energy; however, aging infrastructure must be modernized to meet evolving environmental and operational requirements. The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers (USACE) operates 90 large Kaplan turbines within the Federal Columbia River Power System, many approaching the end of their service life. At Ice Harbor Dam in Washington State, an adjustable-blade turbine was installed at Unit 3 (U3AB) and evaluated using autonomous Sensor Fish (SF) technology to assess hydraulic conditions relevant to fish passage. Unlike conventional fixed-blade turbine designs, the adjustable-blade configuration allows modification of blade positioning to mitigate adverse hydraulic conditions associated with fish injury. SF data showed that U3AB improved hydraulic conditions for fish passage relative to the baseline turbine. The highest combined median value of the nadir pressure occurred during the lowest (Lower 1%) operation (144.8 kPa), while the lowest occurred during the Generator Limit (Upper 1%) operation (120.0 kPa), indicating reduced barotrauma risk. Across operations, ≤1.0% of SF releases experienced nadir pressures below 64.1 kPa, and modeled barotrauma-related mortal injury probabilities remained low (0.78–2.26%). U3AB demonstrated lower percentages of severe acceleration events (≥95 g) in its runner region (5.2–9.9%) compared to the baseline turbine. Strike metrics and SF measurements further indicated high estimated 48-h fish survival rates of 96.1–98.7% across turbine operations based on the velocity-based strike metric ( M V ), consistent with live-fish survival estimates. These results demonstrate that U3AB met its design goals for improved fish passage while maintaining operational efficiency and support modernization of aging hydropower infrastructure with reduced ecological impacts.

Urban and industrial water systems are neglected renewable energy source, even as demand for energy has risen and sustainability targets push back on fossil fuel power generation. In order to fill this research gap, this study aims to design and optimise the vertical free-fall water flow from reinforced concrete (RC) tanks for electricity generation through the crossflow hydro turbine. The impact of blade quantity (15, 25, and 30 blades) and blade angles (20°, 25°, 30°, 35°, 40°, and 45°) on turbine performance was evaluated. A 3D model of the turbine was created in SolidWorks, including detailed blade-geometry considerations to optimise the turbine. The pressure distribution and the efficiency of energy conversion were investigated using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation in ANSYS Fluent based on 36 configurations of turbine, where the inlet velocity was kept constant at 18.26 m/s (corresponding to a head of 0.8 m). The results indicated that both a low blade angle (20°–25°) and a high blade number (30 blades) showed the highest performance, and the 30-blade, 25° configuration generated the maximum pressure of 319,336.3 Pa, torque of 3257.230 Nm, angular velocity of 22.687 rad/s and power output of 73.896 kW. The results serve as a comparative benchmark for future experimental and practical studies into the generation of small-scale hydropower. The correct positioning of the outlet of the RC tank with respect to the turbine is identified as a critical parameter for reducing losses and improving efficiency in successive design versions.

The growing share of intermittent sources, such as solar and wind power, in the electricity mix has heightened the need for storage systems capable of mitigating fluctuations in supply and ensuring energy security. Among the available technologies, pumped-storage hydropower (PSH) plants stand out; they store energy by pumping water to an elevated reservoir, allowing it to be used later for electricity generation. However, topographical and environmental constraints can limit their implementation. In this context, this study proposed an alternative storage system based on the principles of pumped-storage hydroelectric plants, in which the upper reservoir is replaced by a pressurized reservoir. In this configuration, energy is stored through the compression of the air confined within the reservoir. The study involved mathematical modeling of the pumping and turbine stages, followed by computational simulation using the Python programming language. The results made it possible to analyze the temporal evolution of operational variables and to evaluate the efficiency of the proposed system, showing that the system, in its current configuration, exhibited lower efficiency than conventional pumped-storage hydroelectric plants. Thus, this research presents the concept of the system and establishes a foundation for future studies.

This study reassesses the green-energy transition in Kazakhstan, the Kyrgyz Republic, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan using the latest harmonised capacity data available in 2026 and a structured review of 17 Scopus-indexed studies published in 2020-2026. The empirical design separates scale, speed and technological composition rather than treating installed renewable capacity as a single measure of transition maturity. Three indicators are calculated for 2023-2025: compound annual capacity growth, each country's contribution to regional capacity additions, and a technology-concentration index based on hydropower, solar and wind shares. Regional renewable capacity rose from 17.636 GW in 2023 to 25.482 GW in 2025, an increase of 44.5%. Uzbekistan accounted for 86.4% of the net regional addition and reached 10.027 GW, while solar and wind represented 75.6% of its renewable portfolio. Kazakhstan retained the most technologically balanced portfolio, whereas the Kyrgyz Republic and Tajikistan remained strongly hydro-dependent. The results show that capacity expansion and transition quality are analytically distinct. A durable transition requires grid reinforcement, storage, flexible dispatch, competitive procurement, credible investment rules and regional electricity exchange. The article proposes a system-value framework in which new renewable capacity is evaluated by delivered generation, reliability, curtailment, carbon intensity and integration cost rather than by megawatts alone.

Between 2019 and 2025, solar generation on Pakistan's grid grew fourteen-fold, from 2.6 TWh to 36.6 TWh, reaching 22.5% of grid output and peaking at roughly one-third of monthly generation. Ember data through March 2026 show the boom continuing: solar supplied 32.3% of total generation in the first quarter of 2026 (12.1 of 37.5 TWh), overtaking coal, gas, nuclear and hydropower to become the single largest source on the system. This paper assembles regulatory, trade and generation data to explain why one of the world's fastest solar transitions occurred in a fiscally distressed power system, and to characterise who is leaving the grid and how. We document two distinct solar booms. The first is a metered, net-metering boom (6.1 GW and over 378,000 consumers by June 2025), concentrated overwhelmingly, with roughly 85% of capacity, in the six best-performing distribution jurisdictions, and driven by tariffs that more than doubled in three years. The second is a largely invisible, off-grid and behind-the-meter boom, revealed by the gap between roughly 40 GW of cumulative panel imports since FY2020 and the much smaller registered capacity, and concentrated where service failure is severest: utilities whose monitored load shedding exceeds 8–10 h per day, transmission and distribution losses approach 40%, and recovery falls to 39%. Using NEPRA's FY2024–25 performance evaluation data, the study shows that formal grid defection tracks affordability stress in well-served, higher-income regions, while reliability-driven defection elsewhere bypasses the regulatory system entirely. The findings extend the utility death-spiral literature to a developing-country setting in which exit operates through two channels with opposite visibility, and carry direct implications for the December 2025 shift from net metering to net billing.

Contexte. Les systèmes électriques d’Afrique subsaharienne connaissent une transformation rapide : hausse de la capacité de production, croissance soutenue de la demande et réformes institutionnelles. Pourtant, les méthodes de gestion conçues pour les réseaux fortement maillés des pays industrialisés s’appliquent mal à des réseaux faiblement maillés, à dominante hydroélectrique et pauvres en données. Objectif. Cet article propose GEART (Gestion Énergétique Adaptative du Réseau de Transport), un cadre méthodologique destiné aux gestionnaires de réseau de transport (GRT) des économies émergentes. Méthode. Le cadre articule quatre piliers — exploitation adaptative, planification dynamique, coordination institutionnelle et fiabilité opérationnelle — mesurés par six indicateurs (IES, IDR, ICES, IRP, TDO, ICI) agrégés en un indice global. Il est validé par une étude de cas longitudinale (2018–2026) menée au sein de la SONATREL, GRT du Cameroun. Résultats. La mise en service progressive de Nachtigal (420 MW, 2024–2025) révèle une fenêtre critique durant laquelle l’indice de robustesse de la planification (IRP) est resté inférieur à 1, la production disponible excédant la capacité d’évacuation effective. L’indice d’évacuation sécurisée du RIS est estimé à 85–90 % sur cette période. Ces résultats confirment que la fiabilité du système dépend d’abord de la qualité de gestion du transport. Originalité. GEART intègre la dimension institutionnelle au même rang que les dimensions techniques et fournit un langage commun de mesure pour l’étalonnage des GRT africains. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- Power systems in Sub-Saharan Africa are expanding rapidly, yet management methods designed for heavily meshed grids in industrialised countries fit poorly with weakly meshed, hydro-dominated and data-scarce networks. This paper proposes GEART (Adaptive Energy Management of the Transmission Network), a four-pillar framework for transmission system operators (TSOs) in emerging economies — adaptive operation, dynamic planning, institutional coordination and operational reliability — measured by six indicators aggregated into a global index. The framework is validated through an eight-year longitudinal case study (2018–2026) at SONATREL, Cameroon’s TSO, covering the staged commissioning of the 420 MW Nachtigal hydropower plant, the PRRTERS reinforcement programme and the Cameroon–Chad interconnection (PIRECT). Results show a critical window in which the planning robustness index remained below 1 and confirm that system reliability depends primarily on transmission management quality rather than on installed generation alone.

To advance the modernization of power systems, the role of hydropower has transitioned from mere energy generation to serving as both a primary energy provider and a critical flexibility resource. However, conventional day-ahead scheduling methodologies for cascaded hydropower often prove inadequate in mitigating the short-term power imbalances induced by renewable energy variability, primarily due to an oversimplification of operational constraints. To fully harness the regulatory potential of hydropower, this paper proposes an optimal day-ahead scheduling strategy for a cascade hydro-wind-solar-thermal-storage system incorporating hybrid pumped storage (HPS). First, leveraging the operational characteristics of HPS, this study evaluates its capacity for renewable energy accommodation and identifies key challenges in power balancing from the perspectives of water resource management and energy dispatch. Second, a collaborative optimization framework is established. By introducing the concept of an “allowable reservoir water level fluctuation range” within the day-ahead dispatch cycle, the framework constrains the deviation between the actual end-of-period water level and its predefined target, thereby ensuring strict adherence to medium-to-long-term operational boundaries. Finally, case studies conducted on a modified IEEE 33-node system demonstrate that the integration of HPS significantly enhances system regulation capabilities. The results confirm that the proposed strategy contributes to secure, economical, and low-carbon grid operation while maintaining reservoir sustainability.

Joint refill of cascade reservoirs must balance flood control safety against water conservation and hydropower generation, yet conventional operation applies fixed flood-limiting water levels that ignore the time-varying nature of flood risk within a flood season. Existing refill optimization models rarely embed flood season staging as time-varying operational constraints, which limits their ability to capture stage-dependent flood risk and refill opportunity, particularly in cascades headed by a large regulating reservoir. This study develops a framework that identifies flood season stages via the mean change-point method across multiple hydrological stations, transforms the stage boundaries into time-varying water-level constraints, and embeds them in a genetic algorithm-based joint refill optimization model for the Dadu River cascade in southwestern China. Applied to a 65-year inflow record, the framework consistently identifies early August as the main-to-post-flood transition and a secondary autumn flood rebound from mid-September to early October. Relative to the design scheme based on approved conventional operating rules and fixed flood-limiting water level controls, the optimized operation increases the multi-year average total generation of the five-station cascade by 10.08%, from 507.98 × 108 kWh to 559.16 × 108 kWh, while achieving a 100% filling rate at the leading Shuangjiangkou reservoir and maintaining acceptable flood storage during the post-flood period. By demonstrating that within-year inflow trend substantially modulates refill outcomes, especially when annual inflow volumes are comparable, the framework offers differentiated refill strategies and a transferable approach for cascade systems with newly commissioned leading reservoirs in monsoon-driven basins.

The data measures how year-on-year domestic hydropower generation shocks are physically absorbed through four key utility margins: cross-border imports, fossil-fuel generation backup, alternative generation sources, and lost end-user consumption. 2. FILE INVENTORY AND STRUCTURE * README.txt: This documentation file. * Mabea2026_AfricaElectricity_RawData.csv: Primary compilation of raw annual physical electricity accounts (in TWh) and carbon intensity indicators (g CO2/kWh) extracted from Our World in Data (Ember/Energy Institute). * Mabea2026_AccountingIdentities_Processed.csv: Finalized estimation dataset containing the first-differenced, normalized operational variables calculated via equation (8) in the manuscript. * Mabea2026_SAPP_Analysis_Code.do: Fully commented master script executing equations (10) through (17). 3.
