Abstract Optimal operation of inter-basin reservoir groups is the key to improving the regulation capacity of the new power system. Taking the XX Water Diversion Project as an example, based on the water diversion project data and hydrological station data, this paper uses methods such as area ratio interpolation to calculate and analyze the annual/period runoff and power generation at each dam site under different water inflow frequencies, and quantitatively assesses the spatiotemporal impact of water diversion on the runoff and power generation of typical cascade hydropower stations in the southwest. The results show that water diversion significantly alters the temporal and spatial distribution of runoff, and the degree of spatial impact decreases successively with the increase of the distance from the water diversion hub and the intervention of downstream inter-basin confluence. Temporally, water diversion significantly aggravates water shortages in the dry season, and the runoff at the Shuangjiangkou section of the Dadu River during the dry season decreases by as much as 86.24%. Affected by runoff attenuation, the power generation of cascade hydropower stations has significantly decreased. Among them, the power generation loss of the Yalong River and Dadu River cascade hydropower stations gradually expands as the natural runoff decreases, while the damage to the power generation of the Jinsha River cascade hydropower stations shows a complex mechanism, and the peak of annual power generation loss occurs in the dry year rather than the extremely dry year. Overall, under the influence of water diversion, the intra-annual redistribution of runoff and the power generation process further intensifies the seasonal contradiction in power supply guarantee of the basin.

Biomass-based electricity can provide dispatchable, renewable flexibility that complements variable renewables and hydro resources, linking grid reliability with the circular bioeconomy through the valorization of biological residues and by-products. This study assesses whether biomass generation behaves as an operational flexibility service in a hydro-dominated power system using daily data for Colombia from 2017 to 2025. The stress of the system was operationalized system stress as net load pressure daily system demand minus hydropower, wind, and solar generation—capturing the residual need for dispatchable supply. We estimate generalized additive models that flexibly control for long-run changes, cyclic annual seasonality, and day-of-week patterns. The generalized additive model was estimated with a first-order autoregressive AR(1) correction, which accounts for serial dependence between consecutive daily residuals. Results show a robust positive association between biomass generation and system stress, consistent with biomass scaling up when hydro and variable renewables are less able to meet demand. Spot price effects are statistically significant but secondary once operational stress and temporal structure are considered. An exploratory stress–season interaction surface suggests that biomass responsiveness varies across the year, indicating seasonal regimes in which bio-based flexibility becomes more valuable. The findings position biomass electricity as a cleaner, circular-bioeconomy flexibility resource that can support resilience in hydro-dependent grids facing renewable variability and seasonal constraints.

Abstract To address the multi-objective conflicts between power generation benefits and the guarantee of minimum system output in the joint dispatch of inter-basin hydropower clusters, as well as the challenges in model solving, a multi-objective optimization dispatch model for inter-basin hydropower clusters was developed. This model comprehensively considers constraints such as water balance, reservoir water level control, and hydraulic connectivity, and incorporates the relative membership fuzzy optimization method to achieve a unified evaluation of multiple objectives. Based on this, a two-stage solution framework was proposed, consisting of “initial solution via iterative approximation of the DDDP-optimization via local search correction.” Taking 27 power stations across the Jinsha River (partial section), Yalong River, Wujiang River, and the Three Gorges-Gezhouba cascade as the study subjects, a case study was conducted using long-term runoff data from 1959 to 2012. The results indicate that the developed model and solution method can effectively yield stable and reliable dispatch plans. A significant trade-off exists between the power generation objective and the minimum output objective: when the weight of power generation is too high, minimum output decreases significantly. Conversely, when the weights are close, both power generation benefits and output stability can be balanced. The comprehensive optimal solutions are primarily concentrated in the weight equilibrium range. These findings provide a reference for the coordinated dispatch of hydropower clusters across river basins and for enhancing the power grid’s supply security.

Preface The 2026 International Conference on Hydropower Systems and Energy Engineering (HSEE 2026) took place from July 31 to August 2, 2026, in Lhasa, China. At a time of rapid change in energy systems worldwide, the meeting brought together researchers and engineers to share work on hydropower and related energy topics. Presentations and discussions addressed intelligent plant control, digital modeling of energy networks, multi-source complementary generation, and the integration of energy storage. Questions of plant safety, environmental impact, and the physical principles behind efficient power conversion were also central to the program. In linking basic science to practical engineering, HSEE 2026 gave participants a welcome chance to exchange ideas and consider paths toward cleaner and more dependable energy systems. HSEE 2026 featured three distinguished keynote speakers whose work spanned catalysis, integrated energy systems, and advanced functional materials. Prof. Li Neng from Wuhan University of Technology presented “Creation of Highly Efficient Catalysts for Green Hydrogen Electrochemical Preparation,” outlining new catalyst designs that support clean hydrogen production. Prof. Lu Hao of Xinjiang University spoke on “Research on Optimal Operation of Multi-Energy Complementary Integrated Energy Systems Considering Electricity-Hydrogen-Carbon Synergy,” examining coordinated low-carbon strategies for modern power networks. Prof. Wang Yuanhao from Shenzhen Polytechnic University delivered “Construction of Metal-Organic Framework/Graphene Oxide Composites and Their Energy Storage Properties,” reporting recent advances in novel materials for energy storage. Collectively, these talks tied fundamental material physics to pressing energy engineering problems, strengthening the meeting's emphasis on practical pathways toward more sustainable and efficient power systems. We extend our warm thanks to everyone who contributed to the success of HSEE 2026. The active participation of delegates, the guidance of the program committee, and the tireless work of volunteers all played an essential part in making this gathering productive and memorable. We are equally grateful to the keynote speakers for their inspiring lectures and to the authors for sharing their recent findings. We look forward to seeing the ideas exchanged here lead to further advances in sustainable energy engineering. List of Committee Member is available in this PDF.

Giant cascade hydropower station systems (GCHSS) function as basin-scale regulating infrastructures and coordinate multiple utilization objectives, including power generation, at the medium-term scale. Meanwhile, with large-scale wind and photovoltaic (PV) integration, hydropower objectives are shifting from prioritizing energy benefits to balancing energy and peak-shaving benefits. However, the medium-term trade-off and synergy mechanisms between these benefits, along with the peak-shaving performance of the GCHSS subject to basin-wide comprehensive utilization requirements, remain insufficiently clarified. To address this gap, this study proposes a research framework. First, hydropower output is classified by its role in peak shaving. Second, peak-shaving evaluation indicators are established to characterize peak-shaving effectiveness and capacity, together with net load shape indicators to describe peak-shaving demand characteristics. Then, a peak-shaving optimization model is formulated from a power-system perspective to identify critical transitions between energy and peak-shaving benefits. Finally, a bi-level peak-shaving operation optimization model is developed from a cascade-operation perspective. It coordinates medium- and short-term operations and improves peak-shaving benefits while meeting basin-wide comprehensive utilization requirements. A case study of the GCHSS in the upper Yellow River shows that: (1) As hydropower energy increases, the relationship between energy benefits and peak-shaving benefits evolves from coordination to competition. (2) A larger maximum regulation capacity, or net load curves characterized by higher mean levels, lower volatility, steeper gradients, and wider peaks, leads to a broader synergistic range between the two benefits. (3) The optimal generation levels for balancing the two benefits in spring, summer, autumn, and winter are 60%, 56%, 63%, and 66% of the corresponding theoretical maximum generation, respectively. (4) the GCHSS reduces the peak–valley difference, tracking pressure, and volatility of the residual load by 18.64%, 20.44%, and 14.34%, respectively, with stronger peak-shaving performance from summer to early autumn and weaker performance in mid- to late winter.

In the Northwest Territories (NWT), end-of-season snowpack volume is an essential indicator for spring flood potential, wildfire risk, and hydroelectric power generation, and it underpins cold region hydrological research and monitoring. This study presents 31 years of previously unpublished manual snow survey data from Canada’s NWT and investigates trends in end-of-season snow water equivalent (SWE) over time. We then compare SWE trends and magnitudes with ERA5-Land reanalysis data to assess its suitability as an additional data source for snow monitoring. We also extrapolate our analysis to the Mackenzie River basin (MRB) to explore trends and biases for upstream basins. Spearman rank correlation analysis demonstrated strong agreement in SWE trend variability between datasets within the NWT, and a moderately strong agreement for datasets within the MRB. We found that climate variables were the dominant drivers of residuals between datasets. Over the 31-year period, SWE trends exhibited substantial spatial variability within and between sub-basins and ecozones, and most notably, two basins supplying hydropower to NWT communities exhibited opposite trends directionally (Snare River basin decreasing at 4.8 ± 4.9%/decade; Taltson River basin increasing at 4.4 ± 4.3 %/decade). No consistent latitudinal or elevational trends emerged, highlighting the complex, landscape-dependent influence of warming air temperatures on snowpack accumulation. ERA5-Land bias was statistically independent of snow magnitude for most basins and ecoregions, which enhances confidence in the use of this product during high and low snowpack years. These findings are relevant to decision makers who need an improved understanding on how SWE trends are changing at a basin scale. These results demonstrate that the combined use of manual snow surveys and gridded reanalysis datasets can be used to strengthen long-term snow monitoring and research in the NWT.

CERRA-Based Meteorological Cutouts for High-Resolution Wind Energy Modelling with PyPSA-Spain This repository provides high-resolution meteorological cutouts derived from the Copernicus European Regional ReAnalysis (CERRA) dataset for wind energy assessment and power system modelling in the Iberian Peninsula. The cutouts have been specifically prepared for use with PyPSA-Spain and the atlite framework. The cutout includes only the meteorological variables required by atlite to model onshore and offshore wind generation using logarithmic vertical wind speed extrapolation: Wind speed at 100 m above ground level (wnd100m). Surface roughness length (roughness). The original CERRA data are provided on a Lambert conformal grid. To ensure compatibility with atlite, the relevant variables are regridded to a regular latitude-longitude grid with a spatial resolution of 0.05° (approximately 5 km). Wind speed is regridded using bilinear interpolation, while surface roughness is interpolated using the nearest-neighbor method to preserve abrupt spatial variations associated with changes in land cover and surface features. A continuous hourly time series is constructed by combining CERRA analysis fields, available every three hours (00:00, 03:00, 06:00, …, 21:00 UTC), with short-range forecast fields. Specifically, the intermediate hours are obtained from the first two forecast lead times (+1 h and +2 h) of the preceding analysis cycle. Users wishing to rely exclusively on CERRA analysis fields should configure PyPSA-Spain to use a time step of 3 hours. The dataset is distributed as an atlite-compatible NetCDF cutout and retains the era5 module identifier to ensure compatibility without requiring modifications to the atlite code. Data Source All meteorological data are derived exclusively from CERRA, available through the Copernicus Climate Data Store: https://cds.climate.copernicus.eu/ Configuration and Usage To use this dataset in PyPSA-Spain, the CERRA cutout must be explicitly selected in the configuration file for the onwind and/or offwind technologies. Since the CERRA cutout contains only wind-related meteorological variables, an additional standard atlite cutout must be specified as the default_cutout to provide the meteorological inputs required for other technologies and applications, such as solar PV, hydropower, and temperature-dependent processes. These default cutouts can be obtained from the PyPSA-Eur cutout repository. For example, the YAML configuration file can be modified to run a simulation for the year 2023 as follows: alite: default_cutout: europe-2023-sarah3-era5 renewable: onwind: cutout: iberia-2023-cerra resource: method: wind interpolation_method: logarithmic offwind: cutout: iberia-2023-cerra resource: method: wind interpolation_method: logarithmic Licensing and Attribution The cutouts are distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) licence, subject to the attribution requirements associated with the original data sources. Users of these cutouts should acknowledge the original CERRA dataset and cite their corresponding sources in scientific publications and derived products. Availability of additional cutouts Cutouts for other European regions can be prepared upon request. Interested users are encouraged to contact the corresponding author for further information.

Floods, hydrological variability, agricultural losses, rural business interruption, and inequitable access to water and energy are interconnected development challenges.They are frequently addressed in separate planning and financing processes, which reduces the likelihood of a coordinated risk-reduction and recovery approach.This paper introduces an integrated approach that connects the flood-risk assessment and early warning with the planning of reservoirs and hydropower facilities (if applicable), agricultural security, climate-resilient agricultural cultivation, continuity of livestock and fisheries, agricultural storage and access to markets, sustainable financing, and public responsibility.This paper has been more scientific, as some of the data were obtained virtually over two consecutive years through the ARSET NASA training program.The main implementation case is the Gandak River Basin, Gopalganj district, Bihar, India, with a proposed pilot.

As AI, semiconductors, data centers, electric vehicles, and battery industries expand rapidly, electricity is becoming a critical resource for national industrial competitiveness. In the past, industrial zones were typically developed first and electricity infrastructure was subsequently built to serve them. The rise of electricity-intensive advanced industries is beginning to reverse this logic: companies increasingly consider not only access to markets and labor, but also whether large quantities of electricity can be secured reliably—and whether that electricity can be produced with low carbon emissions.This article examines Sweden as an interesting example of this transition. Sweden’s advantage lies not simply in producing abundant electricity, but in combining hydropower, nuclear power, and wind power with grid development and industrial-location policy. In particular, Sweden has increasingly sought to attract electricity-intensive industries to regions where power generation is abundant, especially in the north, effectively turning the geography of electricity production into an industrial-policy asset. For Korea, which is pursuing major investments in semiconductors, AI data centers, batteries, and other electricity-intensive industries, the Swedish experience suggests an important shift in perspective: electricity should no longer be treated merely as infrastructure supporting industrial policy, but as a strategic asset that helps determine where future industries can develop.

This dataset accompanies the manuscript "Water storage dynamics in a regulated Andean lake system: hydroclimatic variability and hydropower generation in Laguna del Laja, Chile." It contains 25 annual observations (2000–2024) and six study variables. Values are carried over from the authors' supplied final raw-data workbook without numerical alteration

This study uses OSeMOSYS through MUIO to compare three pathways for Viet Nam’s electricity system, reporting results for 2026–2050. All scenarios share final electricity demand and technology costs. Business as usual (BAU) retains minimum fossil-generation requirements. Renewable expansion (RE_EXP) removes these requirements and introduces a minimum eligible renewable generation share reaching 75% in 2050, covering wind, solar PV and biomass. COAL_TR adds restrictions that progressively reduce coal generation to zero by 2050 and prohibit new coal capacity from 2031. Solar and wind dominate the transition portfolios, complemented by hydropower, biomass and nuclear generation. By 2050, installed generation capacity reaches approximately 787 GW in both transition scenarios, compared with 479.7 GW under BAU. Annual direct CO₂ emissions fall to 44.5 Mt under RE_EXP and 20.8 Mt under COAL_TR, compared with 718.6 Mt under BAU. Cumulative emissions over 2026–2050 are 72.51% and 76.82% lower than BAU, respectively. Cumulative capital investment reaches USD 1,436.2 billion under RE_EXP and USD 1,461.3 billion under COAL_TR, compared with USD 1,089.1 billion under BAU. Additional investment therefore amounts to USD 347.1 billion and USD 372.2 billion. These undiscounted capital requirements exclude fuel expenditure, operating costs and salvage values and do not establish differences in total system costs or abatement costs. The shared renewable-share endpoint produces different cumulative emissions, highlighting the importance of fossil-generation constraints and transition timing. Zero coal generation also remains distinct from complete coal-capacity retirement and zero direct emissions. Comparisons with BAU reflect the combined scenario packages, including removal of fossil-generation floors. The single-region model and 20 representative time slices do not resolve regional transmission constraints or hourly reliability, while pumped-hydro deployment has no national potential ceiling.

This study uses the CLEWs model to assess Nepal’s energy, land, water, and agricultural systems from 2020 to 2050 under three scenarios: Business as Usual (BAU), Green Transition Target (GTT), and Climate-Induced Impact (CII). The results show that electricity, water, and crop demand will increase significantly by 2050. The GTT scenario offers a cleaner energy pathway by expanding hydropower and solar power while phasing out diesel-based electricity generation. However, the CII scenario highlights the risks of reduced crop production and increased dependence on food imports due to climate impacts. Overall, the study highlights the need to balance renewable energy development, food security, water management, and climate resilience to support Nepal’s sustainable development. This report uses OSeMOSYS to examine India’s electricity-sector pathways through 2050 under three scenarios: business-as-usual (BAU), 40% electrification (E40) and 60% electrification (E60). It assesses generation capacity, electricity generation, investment requirements and CO₂ emissions while evaluating targets for non-fossil capacity, nuclear power and pumped-storage hydropower. The results highlight how higher electrification, constrained clean-energy capacity and growing demand can lead to a coal and emissions rebound. The report discusses policy measures to support sustained decarbonisation, including emissions constraints, nuclear capacity expansion and energy storage.

This study assesses the financial viability of the Chainpur Seti Hydropower Project, Nepal using the FINPLAN financial model. The analysis focuses on how annual energy generation, electricity tariffs, and financing parameters influence the bankability of the project. As a peaking run-of-river project with five hours of daily peaking capacity, the project's viability depends on reliable generation, and the value of electricity tariff provided during high-demand periods. The analysis examines the sensitivity of project revenues and financial returns to the investors. The assessment also highlights the importance of realistic revenue projections and robust financial structuring. In summary, the Chainpur Seti Hydropower Project, a large scale project can contribute to Nepal's energy security and regional development. However, its long-term financial sustainability depends on hydrological resilience leading to resilient energy generation, revenue generation, appropriate tariff arrangements, and financing conditions that support adequate returns while maintaining debt-servicing capacity. With the increasing global demand for renewable energy, micro-hydropower has gained attention due to its low environmental impact and suitability for decentralized deployment. Successful installation, however, requires sufficient hydraulic head and stable water flow. Water drop structures in irrigation canals provide elevation differences, making them promising sites for micro-hydropower generation. Yet their large quantity and wide spatial distribution render traditional manual surveys inefficient and labor-intensive, limiting comprehensive planning and assessment. To address this challenge, this study proposes an automated identification framework that integrates a quantum geographic information system (QGIS) and YOLO with image recognition technology. Nationwide irrigation canal spatial data are first imported into QGIS to establish a canal database. Canal imagery is then extracted and preprocessed to construct a dataset for object detection. The YOLO model is applied to automatically identify drop structures from the exported images. The results are converted into geospatial data with spatial coordinates and reintegrated into QGIS for visualization and spatial management. The results show that the proposed approach significantly improves the efficiency and positional accuracy of drop structure identification. The automated workflow reduces labor costs and operational risks associated with manual field surveys and provides reliable spatial references for preliminary micro-hydropower site selection. This framework supports the reuse of existing water infrastructure and enhances sustainable energy planning. Future work may incorporate power generation potential evaluation models or integrate UAV imagery to further improve assessment precision and practical applicability.

The use of renewable energy sources like solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal, natural gas, as well as diesel in hybrid power systems leads to problems of stability of frequency and voltage arising from volatile generation and rapid loads changing. The study focuses on issues connected with frequency and voltage stability in two-area hybrid power system simulated in the MATLAB/Simulink environment. Three standard controllers such as PI, PD, and PID are applied for Load Frequency Control (LFC) and Automatic Voltage Regulation (AVR) in order to enhance the system performance. In the study, the behavior of the applied controllers is evaluated with respect to major dynamic parameter of interest, including frequency deviation, voltage deviation, settling time, rise time, overshoot, and undershoot. The simulation results show if one or another controller is able to lessen oscillations occurring in the system and return it back to the nominal condition. The comparative analysis reveals that the PID controller outperforms the PI and PD controllers in terms of overall stability as a consequence of increased controllability and stabilization speed.

Digital handover represents a typical digital application scenario resulting from the deep integration of new-generation information technology and hydropower engineering construction. Aiming at the prominent issues existing in the current handover implementation process, such as model information disruption and inter-stage data discontinuity, this paper proposes a model management technical solution with the core of establishing a bidirectional mapping system for design-construction management structures, based on an analysis of the content of digital handover in hydropower projects and the current status of BIM model management. This solution achieves the structured integration, organic connection, and lossless flow and transmission of model carriers and associated data. Engineering practice verification shows that this solution can break through the data and information barriers between stages, significantly improve the collaboration efficiency and data integration quality during the engineering construction phase, provide a reusable technical paradigm for the full-life-cycle digital management of hydropower projects, and possess important practical reference value for further promoting the digital transformation of the industry.

Hydrogen is a by-product of electrochemical phosphorus removal, but its environmental and economic relevance has rarely been assessed. In this work, two electrochemical routes were evaluated: an Mg-assisted electroless system (AZ31 anode and stainless-steel cathode), expected to favor struvite precipitation, and a current-driven system (Ti/IrO 2 -Ta 2 O 5 anode and stainless-steel cathode), expected to favor Ca-phosphate precipitation. Under the baseline scenario, the current-driven Ca-phosphate-oriented route showed higher environmental impacts than the Mg-assisted route in 16 ReCiPe Midpoint categories. Its environmental performance improved markedly when hydropower was considered, demonstrating that the relative ranking of the two routes is strongly dependent on electricity supply. H 2 generation ranged from 1.9 to 2.7 m 3 H 2 m −3 d −1 , accounting for 10–50% of environmental credits and 69% of the revenue. These values may be improved through continuous gas removal. This study provides experimental evidence of the environmental and economic contribution of H 2 for electrochemical P recovery and identifies further research priorities.

Assessing the future performance of Manitoba hydropower system is challenging due to its complex interconnected river-reservoir network and uncertainty in future water supply and electricity demand. This thesis develops and applies an integrated modelling framework to evaluate climate change impacts on the Manitoba hydropower system under deep inflow uncertainty and changing electricity demand. The first component of this thesis develops MB_HydroSim, an integrated water resources management model of the large-scale river- reservoir system in Manitoba. By incorporating both explicitly defined and implicitly derived operating rules, MB_HydroSim reproduces key system dynamics, including water levels, outflows, and hydropower generation, providing a reliable foundation for climate impact assessment and hydropower generation planning. The second component presents a target-based synthetic streamflow generator that enables the generation of a broad and controlled range of plausible inflow conditions beyond the historical record and the relatively limited range represented by GCM projections. The framework directly targets monthly streamflow magnitude, variability, and seasonality in real space, allowing statistically credible streamflow scenarios to be generated for multisite studies at low computational cost. The third component stress tests the Manitoba hydropower system under a wide range of plausible inflow conditions and historical and future electricity demand scenarios. Results show that dry conditions create greater performance losses than the benefits gained under comparable wet conditions. Higher inflows can improve hydropower generation outcomes, but also increase lake level excursions, indicating a benefit- stability trade-off in the system. Although annual assessments indicate lower expected system stress in the future, they mask important seasonal system behavior; increase in the number of seasons experiencing higher system stress in the future (summer and autumn). Overall, the findings demonstrate that adaptive operational strategies are needed beyond expanding hydropower generation capacity. The contributions of this thesis extend beyond Manitoba. MB_HydroSim provides a transferable example of operation-based simulation for complex, regulated, cold- regions river-reservoir systems. The target streamflow generation framework can be applied to multisite water systems where direct control of streamflow properties is needed for stress testing. The stress-testing framework can be adapted to other hydropower and regulated water systems by redefining system objectives, performance thresholds, and relevant stressors.

Abstract Climate warming accelerates glacier retreat and glacial lake expansion, creating hydropower opportunities while increasing flood hazards. Despite extensive research on glacial lake hazards, assessments of hydropower potential and development suitability remain limited. Here, we quantify the theoretical hydropower potential of 37 glacial lakes in the Poiqu river basin, central Himalaya, by integrating multi‐scenario climate projections with annual lake water budget reconstruction to estimate hydropower‐relevant inflow across four operational stages during 2025–2100 and by deriving available hydraulic heads through hierarchical river network and topographic gradient analyses. We develop a multi‐criteria framework to evaluate environmental, technical, and economic suitability and prioritize lakes. Across four climate scenarios, basin‐wide mean annual generation is projected at about 212.8 GWhr yr −1 during Stage I (risk mitigation, 2025–2030), followed by about 200.6, 197.0, and 194.3 GWhr yr −1 during Stages II–IV (adaptive generation, 2031–2100), respectively. Paqupuco is identified as the top‐priority site, with annual generation potential of about 14.3 GWhr yr −1 and a suitability score of 80.6. At the regional screening scale, modeled operations could reduce the maximum storage of high‐risk lakes, such as Gangxico and Galongco, to about 71% of their initial capacities. Sensitivity analyses indicate that basin‐wide estimates and leading candidates are broadly stable under the tested water budget and weighting assumptions. By linking hydropower resource assessment with climate‐adaptive hazard governance, this study provides a regional screening framework for jointly evaluating clean energy opportunities and glacial lake outburst flood mitigation in glacierized mountain regions.

Harnessing the power of water to generate electricity is one of the most cost-effective and sustainable methods of energy production. Small hydropower plants are gaining prominence due to their ability to generate electricity with lower hydraulic heads and smaller flow rates, making them suitable for a wider range of applications. However, the growing global population and its associated demands for water for drinking, agriculture, and industrial purposes are putting increasing pressure on rivers. It is crucial to strike a balance between utilizing river waters for hydropower generation and preserving its availability for essential human needs. The study explored and assessed the small-scale hydropower potentials in the Vhembe District Municipality. The study used geographical and spatial information to identify potential sites for small scale hydropower projects. The study also considered several factors, such as the availability of water, the topography of the area, and the environmental impact of hydropower development. The study identified significant potential for small-scale hydropower development within the Vhembe District Municipality. It pinpointed several promising sites with minimal environmental impact. Developing small-scale hydropower in this area is presented as a viable option that could contribute to the local economy and South Africa's green energy transition. The study recommends that the Vhembe District Municipality further explore this potential and develop a plan for sustainable small-scale hydropower development in the region. These findings can inform similar projects in the region and beyond, becoming a valuable contribution to the national understanding of small-scale hydropower potential in South Africa.

This article investigates the feasibility of implementing pumped-storage hydropower (PSH) systems within the existing hydropower plants (HPPs) of the Drin River cascade in Albania. Currently, five HPPs are operational along the Drin River, two of which are managed by private operators, while the remaining three are operated by the public utility “KESH sh.a”. Increasing climate variability necessitates adaptive operational measures to enhance the safety and resilience of these hydropower assets. In parallel, the rapid development of variable renewable energy sources, such as photovoltaic and wind power, has intensified interest in large-scale energy storage solutions. The study evaluates a case scenario involving the installation of a 200 MW pumped-storage system between two existing reservoirs in the Drin River cascade. Based on a hydrological year characterized by high rainfall, the results indicate that the proposed system could reduce downstream discharge by up to 30% while producing approximately 28 GWh of net electrical energy. Beyond energy generation, the assessment highlights broader system-level benefits, including improved flood risk management, enhanced climate resilience, and optimized hydropower operation. The findings suggest that pumped-storage integration could play a strategic role in supporting Albania’s energy transition and strengthening the operational flexibility of the Drin River hydropower system.

This study investigates the potential of river water energy in Magelang District as an alternative source of electricity. The research method includes measuring the river’s width, depth, and flow velocity, followed by calculating the discharge. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations were used to evaluate the performance of a Savonius turbine with NACA 6409 9% and NACA 0012 blades. The novelty of this research lies in optimizing Savonius turbine efficiency by assessing the influence of different blade geometries on turbine performance in river applications. Simulation results show that blade geometry significantly affects water flow dynamics, causing velocity spikes at the blade tips and varying pressure distributions between the two profiles. Furthermore, the study highlights substantial turbulence downstream of the turbine. These findings provide critical insights for enhancing Savonius turbine design, improving river water energy utilization, and offering practical solutions for renewable power generation in Magelang District

The Toladan River, located in Jayapura Regency, Papua, offers promising opportunities for renewable energy development, particularly small-scale micro-hydropower systems. Accurate estimation of dependable flow is essential for determining hydropower feasibility and sustainable energy planning. This study analyzes the dependable flows of the Toladan River using field-based discharge measurements from three observation points and employing a flow-duration-curve (FDC) statistical approach. Discharge measurements were obtained using the float method, supported by cross-sectional geometry assessments at each site. Results show that average discharges at the three observation points were 0.382 m³/s, 0.448 m³/s, and 0.654 m³/s, respectively, reflecting significant variations in channel dimensions. These values were statistically processed to estimate dependable flow rates at exceedance levels of Q50, Q70, and Q90. The analysis indicates that Q90 dependable discharge remains adequate for small-scale micro-hydropower development. Overall, this study demonstrates that the Toladan River provides a stable flow regime conducive to micro-hydropower generation, offering essential baseline data to support renewable energy planning in Papua

The global demand for artificial intelligence (AI) is fuelling a rapid expansion of data infrastructure, an industry that is notoriously water-intensive. This growth creates a critical, yet understudied, nexus between digital expansion and hydrological systems, particularly in ecologically vulnerable regions. This study applies a spatially explicit framework to quantify the water footprint of AI data centres in Brazil, a nation heavily reliant on drought-sensitive hydropower. Our method integrates datasets on data centre locations, regional hydrological cycles, power generation sources and watershed-level water stress indices to model both direct (cooling) and indirect (energy generation) water consumption. Our key finding is that the AI infrastructure cluster in the São Paulo metropolitan region, with an operational IT load of ~550 MW, has an estimated annual water footprint of 16.1 million cubic metres. A significant portion of this, over 46%, is indirect “virtual water” consumed through hydropower generation, establishing a direct feedback loop where data centre demand stresses water and energy systems already compromised by climate change. This article concludes that the environmental cost of AI extends beyond carbon to include water, a cost disproportionately borne by biodiverse regions. We call for a paradigm shift in tech policy and corporate sustainability to include metrics of water neutrality and watershed resilience, in alignment with global sustainability goals.

The S.K.O.O.G. (Skoog Kinetic Orbital Oscillating Generator) system represents the overarching Skoog Architecture for autonomous, zero-fuel maritime propulsion. Within this framework, the Skoog Open Marine Technology (SOMT) initiative facilitates the development and open-source sharing of these innovations. The SKOOG.system is designed to harness the kinetic energy of the ocean wave field, specifically the orbital motion of surface gravity waves, together with available current energy, through turbines positioned at multiple heights in internal hull channels. The harvested energy supplies electrical propulsion for zero-fuel cargo transport. The concept is intended for slow-speed, non-time-sensitive transport where transit time is secondary to zero-emission operation, stable logistics and minimal operating cost. The Skoog Harvester (AWEV — Autonomous Wave Energy Cargo Vessel) represents the functional application of the Skoog Architecture. Within the AWEV system, waves pass through internal hull channels and drive Skoog LFAS (Lift-optimized Archimedes Screw) turbines. The duct walls constrain lateral water motion and guide the flow through the helical rotors. This configuration uses rotary energy conversion rather than a mechanically reciprocating stroke, allowing energy extraction from flow entering either end of the channels. The rotors can operate in either rotational direction, generating mechanical energy that is converted into electricity and supplied to dedicated propulsion units. Propulsion direction is controlled independently of rotor rotation. These channels are arranged in multiple horizontal turbine rows at different depths, where the upper rows receive water from waves reaching openings above the waterline, and the deeper rows interact with near-surface currents and orbital flow beneath the waves. Together, this multi-depth arrangement provides a hybrid approach to energy harvesting from surface wave motion and shallow subsurface flow. Current-energy extraction depends on water movement relative to the vessel, while favourable ocean currents also support route planning and transport. Unlike conventional Archimedes screw turbines, the Skoog LFAS employs a continuously twisted, hydrofoil-based, lift-optimized blade profile along its entire length, designed to generate useful torque from flow in either direction. The overall vessel configuration is designed to support stable operation. The LFAS geometry is designed for oscillating and bidirectional flows, making the same core design applicable not only to wave-driven vessel propulsion but also to tidal and other reversing marine flow systems. “Oscillating” refers to variations in the water motion, rather than a requirement for the vessel or generator assembly to move back and forth. Cargo is carried in a submerged, ballast-stabilized module designed to provide a stable platform with reduced roll and slamming loads, protecting the payload from direct surface-wave impacts. Supporting new Skoog Architecture technologies that address key marine engineering bottlenecks: Skoog IAKKS: A newly developed active ceramic composite coating system, inspired by brake pad technology, with a projected service-life target of 20 years and near-zero fouling under controlled electro-active operation. The system aims to eliminate the need for toxic antifouling paints and reduce the frequency of hull cleaning. Skoog PHST (Passive Hydrostatic Stabilization): A newly engineered passive hydraulic stabilization system supporting magnetic rotor alignment, with the aim of replacing conventional mechanical bearing arrangements and minimizing maintenance. Opposing fluid chambers compensate for shaft vibration, while an outer reference ring provides additional stabilization to support efficient electrical generation and long service life. Skoog DALAS (Dynamically Adaptive Lift-force System): A newly engineered system combining lift-optimized turbine geometry with adaptive mounting. The mounting converts wave-impact loads into controlled linear displacement for energy recovery, cushioning abrupt loads on the turbines and providing an additional source of electricity during energetic wave conditions, including storms. The DALAS geometry is optimized for unidirectional or pulsed flows, with applications in stationary installations such as gravity-driven water channels, outlets and hydropower systems. Skoog Azimuth-DALAS Propulsion: A dual-unit system of steerable, ducted propulsion units based on the same unidirectional DALAS geometry, with one unit mounted at each bow of the submerged module. The configuration is optimized for efficient thrust and low noise within the targeted low-speed, ducted operating regime, with a reduced underwater acoustic footprint as a design objective. The architecture introduces The Skoog Tacking Principle: a novel hydrodynamic navigation method that replaces traditional rudder steering with active thrust vectoring, avoiding rudder-associated drag and enabling energy-optimized crabbing. See The Skoog Tacking Principle section below for a detailed explanation of how this dual-vector system supports bidirectional operation and adapts vessel alignment to changing sea states. See the extended presentation text below for an illustrative energy calculation showing the system’s estimated power output under the specified Pacific Ocean conditions and operating assumptions. Detailed technical reports providing an in-depth analysis of the Skoog Architecture (S.K.O.O.G.), which incorporates the Skoog Open Marine Technology (SOMT) initiative, are available in the attached PDF files in English and Spanish below. Note on Terminology: In the attached technical reports, the integrated systems of the Skoog Architecture—including Skoog AWEV, Skoog LFAS, Skoog IAKKS, Skoog DALAS, Skoog PHST and Skoog RDG—are frequently referred to by their functional acronyms (AWEV, LFAS, IAKKS, DALAS, PHST and RDG) for technical conciseness. .

In the context of increasing renewable energy penetration and the growing challenge of managing non- programmable sources, hydropower remains a strategic asset for the energy transition. However, in decentralised systems such as local energy communities (LECs) or energy islands, surplus electricity cannot always be injected into the grid profitably or consumed immediately on-site, depending on the mix of local end-users. This study investigates a strategy for valorising surplus electricity through on- site green hydrogen production via water electrolysis, using the excess generation from a small-scale hydropower plant in northern Italy. A techno-economic methodology is applied, combining high- resolution energy analysis, the design of a proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyser system, levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH) estimation, and net present value assessment under different feed- in tariff scenarios. Results indicate that the optimal PEM electrolyser capacity for the case study is 95 kW, requiring an additional 1 kW for hydrogen compression. This configuration produces 14,932 kg of green hydrogen annually, achieving an LCOH of €1.71/kg. The opportunity cost of electricity is excluded, as the energy used for electrolysis comes from surplus production with a marginal operational cost of €10/MWh, considered instead of the full market price. The analysis shows that a break-even feed-in tariff of €7.72/kg is needed to match revenues from electricity sales, while an incentive of only €4.20/kg is sufficient when hydrogen is sold at €5.00/kg. These thresholds are significantly lower than current equivalent incentives, highlighting the economic feasibility of the approach. The findings provide policymakers, LECs and energy islands with a practical decision- making framework to support the deployment of distributed green hydrogen systems, thereby enhancing renewable energy integration and utilisation.

Martha Christino1,2* and Michael Craig1,31 School for Environment and Sustainability, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, US2 Climate and Space Sciences and Engineering, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, US3 Industrial and Operations Engineering, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, US*Author to whom any correspondence should be addressed.E-mail: mlchris@umich.eduAbstractAlternative but equally plausible future climate realizations can necessitate different energy system investments, posing a dilemma to practitioners when making investment decisions. Addressing this dilemma requires quantitative methods to synthesize information across climate realizations, which are lacking in the energy systems community. We present a decision-making framework that centers a risk score to quantify variability in resource adequacy (RA) contributions of investments across potential climate realizations. We apply our framework to the Western U.S. power system, with a focus on California RA outcomes, by integrating dynamically downscaled data from five climate models with an RA model that simulates generator outages and optimizes transmission and storage operations. We find investment portfolios can have highly variable RA contributions between climate models; a wind and battery portfolio reduces expected unserved energy (EUE) by 78% in EC-Earth3 but by only 47% in EC-Earth3-Veg, for instance. Our risk score reflects this variability, yielding a risk score of 0.65 for the wind and battery investment, much higher than a risk score of 0.28 for a solar-only investment portfolio that achieves more consistent RA reductions. By combining our risk score with a benefit metric, we identify a frontier of investment options that illuminate trade-offs for decision-makers that synthesize outcomes across plausible climate realizations.1. IntroductionAs anthropogenic climate change worsens, it will increasingly threaten the reliability of energy systems (Craig et al., 2018 , Sundar et al., 2024, Plaga & Bertsch, 2023, Szinai et al., 2024). These threats will add to concerns regarding near-term electricity resource adequacy gaps (North American Electric Reliability Cooperation, 2024, Redefining Resource Adequacy Task Force, 2021, Gurgel et al., 2024). Worsening climate change will also coincide with significant investments in energy systems driving the energy transition (National Academies, 2021).Existing research has established that climate change will affect diverse parts of transmission-scale power systems, including thermal and renewable generation assets, electricity demand, and transmission networks (Yalew et al., 2020, Bartos & Chester, 2015, Craig et al., 2018). Many studies focus on individual parts of power systems and their performance in future climate realizations (Kapica et al., 2024, Perera et al., 2020, Bloomfield et al., 2021,van der Most et al., 2024, Obringer et al., 2020, Auffhammer et al., 2017, Karnauskas et al., 2018, Losada Carreño et al., 2020, Ralston Fonseca et al., 2019, Deroubaix et al., 2021). This approach provides value in understanding isolated impacts, but neglects system-level interactions within the power system, which ultimately drive reliability outcomes (Grochowicz, 2024).Other studies capture such system-level interactions, but only assess climate change impacts on certain parts of power systems (Ralston Fonseca et al., 2021, Turner et al., 2019, Bartos & Chester, 2015, Kozarcanin et al., 2019, Santos da Silva et al., 2021, Schlott et al., 2018, Simoes et al., 2021,Webster et al., 2022). For example, Ralston Fonseca et al. (2021) forecasts climate change impacts on thermal and hydropower generation but not on wind and solar generation. While these studies present valuable insights for decision makers in siloed parts of the power system, they may miss system impacts of weather patterns driven by compounding effects across system parts. For instance, spiking demand compounded by decreased generation potential across generation types can drive major resource adequacy failures (Turner et al. 2019, Busby et al., 2021, Sundar et al. 2023). Thus, capturing the simultaneous impact of climate change across generation types and demand is necessary to model future compound threats (Plaga & Bertsch, 2023, Yalew et al., 2020, Sundar et al., 2023).In response to this need, a growing body of literature examines system operations and capacity expansion needs across generation types and global climate models (Szinai et al., 2024, Sundar et al., 2024, Gernaat et al., 2021, Voisin et al., 2020, Schlott et al., 2018). These studies identify optimal energy system investments (or capacity expansion plans) under multiple future climate realities. Through this exercise, they show the spread of potential adaptation investments across climate uncertainty. For example, Szinai et al. (2024) models optimal capacity expansion given weather from each of 15 global climate models (GCMs). They find the optimal capacity investments by technology can vary by over 40GW between climate models. Similarly, Sundar et al. (2024) find 25 GW or greater differences in capacity investment between climate realizations from the CESM2 Large Ensemble (LENS2) dataset.These studies collectively demonstrate climate change can significantly affect power system investment needs, but that those effects can vary significantly between climate realizations. How, then, can decision-makers translate these insights into action, i.e. into investment decisions? Significant disagreement surrounds future climate realizations and their likelihoods, resulting in deep uncertainty in future climate change (Lehner, 2020). In the presence of this deep climate uncertainty, we cannot assign individual future climate realizations probabilities of occurring. The cascading impact of this deep uncertainty is that we also cannot assign likelihoods of success to power system investment strategies created from different future climate realizations. Therefore, the existing literature creates a “practitioner’s dilemma” in which decision-makers are presented with (potentially significantly) different investment strategies for different climate realizations, presenting an obstacle to climate-informed decision making (Reed et al., 2022).The climate science community has long recognized the existence of a “practitioner’s dilemma” (Barsugli, 2013, Jagannathan et al., 2019). It has proposed derived metrics to synthesize the results of complex climate simulations into smaller sets of options for decision-makers, bridging the gap from study scenarios to actionable information (Reed et al. 2022). Existing energy systems research lacks this type of metric to distill information from across plausible scenarios, inhibiting our understanding of investment portfolio performance across climate realizations. Instead, it often condenses information across climate scenarios by focusing on average outcomes (e.g., Gernaat, 2021) or worst-case models (e.g., Sundar et al., 2024) to provide actionable insights. Given significant variation exists in power system outcomes across different potential climate realizations, a set of investments that perform well under average or worst-case scenarios may not perform well under all climate realizations.To address the practitioner’s dilemma, we introduce a risk score to quantitatively evaluate the resource adequacy performance of investment portfolios across climate realizations. We integrate dynamically downscaled climate data, an hourly open-source resource adequacy model, and a risk-based decision-making framework (Craig et al., 2022, Rahimi et al., 2024, ASSETRA, 2025). The latter presents a risk score that quantifies the consistency of an investment portfolio’s performance across climate realizations. In so doing, our risk score provides decision-makers a methodology to account for deep climate-related uncertainty when making adaptation investment decisions. Although our framework is extensible to other regions, we focus our analysis on California (the US footprint of the CAMX power system region) through midcentury (specifically 2040 to 2050). We focus on California given its recent resource adequacy failures, large power system investments, and experienced impacts from climate change (California Independent System Operator et al., 2021).2. MethodsWe convert dynamically downscaled climate data (Section 2.1) into a series of power system variables (Section 2.2) for input into a resource adequacy model (Section 2.3) with the exiting power system (Section 2.4), then present a risk analysis framework to synthesize our results into actionable information (Section 2.5).2.1 Climate DataOur future climate realizations are taken from five dynamically downscaled climate models from the WUS-D3 dataset spanning the Western United States (Rahimi et al., 2024). Given that our analysis focuses on increasing power systems resource adequacy through mid-century, we use climate realizations from multiple climate models for a single climate scenario, Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 3-7.0. We emphasize models over emissions scenarios because model uncertainty dominates scenario uncertainty through midcentury (Lehner et al., 2020). We specifically use data from five climate models based on those available in WUS-D3 that provide the best accuracy in estimating meteorological variables relevant to the power system: MPI-ESM1-2-HR, TaiESM1, EC-Earth3, EC-Earth3-Veg, MIROC6 (Buster et al., 2024). These models also capture a range of climate sensitivities, from 2.6 to 4.4 degrees Celsius per Watt per meter squared (Massoud et al., 2023). While a larger ensemble would increase the uncertainty space captured in our modeling, given our experimental design with hourly resolution, the five selected models balance computational tractability with capturing uncertainty among models that perform well in power system applications.The use of dynamically downscaled climate models is vital to our analysis for two reasons: (1) they achieve the necessary spatiotemporal resolution for resource adequacy modeling, and (2) they resolve complex terrain features and meso-scale meteorological events that allow for analysis of future weather extremes (Rahimi et al., 2024). The WUS-D3 is dynamically downscaled using the Weather Research and Forecasting model version 4.1.3 (Skamarock et al., 2019). We use hourly 9-km resolution outputs of 2m temperature, 10m wind, surface pressure, specific humidity, downwelling solar radiation, and surface plus subsurface runoff across WECC. These variables are integrated into our generation and demand predictions.2.2 Converting Climate Data to Power System InputsWe convert weather variables from each of our future climate projections into a full suite of power system inputs, specifically into timeseries of demand; solar capacity factors; wind capacity factors; thermal generation derates and forced outage rates; and hydropower generation potential. This conversion is described briefly for each input below and fully detailed in the SI.Electricity demand is projected for future years by a multi-layer perceptron (MLP). The MLP is trained on historic demand and population-weighted temperature and relative humidity from European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts Reanalysis version 5 (ERA5) for each of the twenty-two balancing authorities (BAs) within WECC (Hersbach et al., 2020). Across BAs, we achieve a mean percentage error of under 15%, and the largest five balancing authorities in WECC, which account for over 55% of annual demand, have mean absolute percentage error of under 6% (SI Section 1). Our projections ignore future changes in population and technological change, which we leave to future work and highlight limitations of in our Discussion.Solar and wind capacity factors are calculated on an hourly basis for each grid cell. We calculate solar generation given downwelling solar radiation, temperature, and wind speed at each plant (Jerez et al., 2015). Wind generation accounts for wind speed extrapolated by scaling factor to 100m hub height, surface pressure, and specific humidity (Karnauskas et al., 2018).We calculate thermal generator deratings on an hourly and plant-specific basis. Deratings indicate loss of available capacity due to ambient conditions reducing the operational efficiency of the plant. We specifically quantify deratings for natural gas fired combined cycle, natural gas steam turbine, conventional steam coal, (Loew et al., 2020) and natural gas fired combustion turbine plants (Bartos & Chester, 2015). These plant types account for over 80% of nameplate installed thermal capacity in WECC. Derating equations are not available for internal combustion engines, nuclear, waste/biomass, petroleum coke, and geothermal plants, so we do not quantify deratings for them, but these thermal plants make up only 6.4% of our system capacity. In our work, thermal generation is derated based on location-specific temperature, specific humidity, and/or surface pressure, depending on the generator type (SI Section 5). Temperature dependent forced outage rates are determined by local surface air temperatures from each climate model (Murphy et al., 2020). Wind and solar units have fixed forced outage rates of 5% and battery storage is modeled with a roundtrip efficiency of 85% (Bromley-Dulfano et al., 2021, Cole et al., 2023).We estimate available hydropower generation on a monthly basis using a linear regression that predicts annual generation based on monthly average runoff (Sundar et al., 2024). Prediction is done regionally based on eight “drought regions,” which represent areas within which hydropower climatology is consistent (Turner et al., 2022). Our regression is trained on ERA5 total runoff, then applied to predict future annual generation from calculated total runoff in the WUS-D3 dataset. To capture seasonality in hydropower operations, we then disaggregate annual to monthly generation potential using historic monthly hydropower generation by drought region (Turner et al., 2022). We exclude the Lower Colorado hydropower region from our analysis because multi-year storage reservoirs in this region mean future management strategies play a larger role than annual meteorological variables in its production, which accounts for less than 3.5%. of average annual hydropower in WECC.2.3 Resource Adequacy ModelingOur key contribution to existing literature is to understand how robust the resource adequacy contribution of an investment portfolio is to different future climate realizations. To quantify the baseline resource adequacy of the existing electricity system and the value of investments in future years across potential future climate realizations, we use a resource adequacy model modified from the publicly available ASSETRA model. ASSETRA uses simulation and optimization methods to compare available electricity supply against demand on an hourly basis. Periods where demand exceeds supply indicate a resource adequacy failure. We run ASSETRA for each of our five climate models (or realizations) separately using demand- and supply-side outputs from Section 2.2. ASSETRA uses a Monte Carlo simulation to sample outages for generators on an hourly basis across a year. ASSETRA provides the timing, magnitude, and duration of unserved energy.To sample stochasticity in outages, we run one hundred independent ASSETRA simulations, then aggregate across simulations. We specifically aggregate simulation results to calculate expected unserved energy (EUE), or the magnitude by which supply exceeds demand, across a year:\(EUE=\ \sum_{h=1}^{8760}{U({G_{h}-L}_{h})}\). Eq1Where h is hour of the year; U is the unserved energy function which is dependent on G, generation, and L, load.ASSETRA runs three heuristics. First, it dispatches hydropower generation from monthly potential to hourly generation. To estimate monthly potential generation by WECC region, we disaggregate monthly generation by drought region (Methods Section 2) to individual plants proportional to each plant’s share of historic generation, then recombine plants by WECC region to obtain monthly potential generation. With the monthly estimate, ASSETRA distributes the monthly generation across every hour of the month proportionally to the spread of forecasted net demand (defined as demand minus wind and solar generation) across the month. Generation in each hour is bounded by the installed capacity in the region. Second, ASSETRA optimizes dispatch of battery and pumped hydropower storage assets based on a greedy storage algorithm, assuming 4 hour batteries and 4 hour pumped hydropower. When demand exceeds available capacity, battery and pumped hydro storage systems discharge to meet shortfalls; at all other times, storage systems pull excess capacity to charge (Bromley-Dulfano et al., 2021). Given the lack of hydrological models, we ignore water availability constraints on pumped hydropower operations. Third, to account for transmission between regions, we use a transport method approximation that places capacity limits on hourly transfers between each region. Electricity flows are then determined by a heuristic that checks every hour of the year in each region to determine when supply shortages occur. If one region has a supply shortage while another has a supply surplus, energy transfers up to the transmission limit and surplus value are allowed (SI Section 9).2.4 Baseline Power System and Investment PortfolioWe run ASSETRA by dividing WECC into three regions used in NERC reliability assessments: DSW, California, and NWPP (North American Electric Reliability Cooperation, 2024). We set demand in each region equal to total demand across the balancing authorities in each region (Section 2.2). To replicate a resource adequacy analysis as would be completed by a utility or NERC, we start by understanding the resource adequacy of the existing power system, which we refer to as our “baseline” system (North American Electric Reliability Cooperation, 2024). Using this baseline system avoids uncertainty related to future siting of power plants, which we leave to future work. To that end, our risk-based methodology can be extended to analyzing future power systems. To parameterize our baseline system, we use existing power plant capacities, types, and locations, and existing interregional transmission capacities (EIA 860 , Ho et al., 2021).Onto our baseline system, we then add investment portfolios and quantify the resulting system resource adequacy. Our investment portfolios include wind, solar, and/or battery storage investments because these resources dominate (make up 97% of) WECC interconnection queues (Energy Markets & Policy, 2025). Our investment portfolios increase installed capacities of solar, wind, and/or storage under different resource combinations across regions, with each investment portfolio equivalent to a 5GW total investment. For instance, the California wind and solar investment includes 2.5GW of solar capacity and 2.5GW of wind capacity in California. To set capacity and location of analyzed investments, our portfolios apply uniform percentage increases to existing wind and solar plant’s capacities in each region. Battery storage is increased by the same percentage, but on a regional basis. This approach is designed to capture technoeconomic and non-technoeconomic factors driving installation decisions in the region by relying on previous investment decisions in the region and is a commonly used approach in the peer-reviewed literature (Sundar et al., 2023, Impram et al., 2020, Zhao et al., 2024, Qiu et al., 2023). In ASSETRA, added investments are accounted for prior to battery storage for each investment portfolio, therefore changes to battery dispatch from increased solar and wind generation are accounted for.2.5 Risk Score and Net BenefitTo address the practitioner’s dilemma in investment decision-making, we calculate a risk score for each investment portfolio. The risk score measures the variability of the investment portfolio’s contribution to system resource adequacy across potential future climate realizations. A high score, for instance, indicates a set of investments have highly variable resource adequacy benefits across potential future climate realizations. PLN has established long-term objectives detailed in Electricity Supply Business Plan for 2021-2030, focusing providing an adequate, reliable, and efficient electricity supply to ensure national energy security such like Hydro Power Plant Development, leveraging Indonesia abundant river system as sustainable energy sources. However, this development is highly sensitive to climate and local hydrological condition. One major external factor is El Niño Southern Oscillation (ENSO). The Sea Surface Temperature NINO represents ENSO data, which serves as an external indicator reflecting changes in sea surface temperature, which are used to identify the occurrence of La Niña or El Niño events. These fluctuations greatly affect river discharge and affecting in electricity generation by Hydropower Plants. This study proposes a machine learning based model that integrates SST NINO 3.4 as dynamic indicators with local climate and hydrological data to improve dependable flow estimation. The SEMMA framework was used for structured analysis, from data exploration to model assessment, applying both Monte Carlo and Latin Hypercube sampling methods. Using SEMMA framework was used for structured analysis, from data exploration to model assessment, applying both Monte Carlo and Latin Hypercube sampling methods. Results show that using SST NINO 3.4 Index help improves model performance across all metrics.

The growing demand for clean energy and the urgency to achieve net-zero emissions by 2050 have placed green hydrogen at the center of decarbonization strategies. This study presents a techno-economic analysis of hydrogen production using surplus electricity from hydropower, particularly during rainy seasons when generation exceeds grid demand. A capacity-based approach is employed to estimate surplus energy, which is then used to calculate the required electrolyzer capacity and the Levelized Cost of Hydrogen (LCOH). Using a 20.8 MW alkaline electrolyzer operating at a 75% capacity factor, and a specific energy consumption of 56.69 kWh/kg H2, the base case LCOH is found to be 3.41 USD/kg. A sensitivity analysis shows that electricity price and capacity factor are the most influential parameters affecting LCOH, followed by electrolyzer scale and installation year. Results suggest that optimizing these parameters can significantly improve the economic feasibility of green hydrogen production. The findings highlight the potential of utilizing existing hydropower infrastructure to support hydrogen generation in a cost-effective and scalable manner, especially in developing regions with abundant but underutilized renewable resources.

This study investigates the impact of El Niño on the inflow dynamics of the Saguling Hydroelectric Power Plant (PLTA), located in West Java, Indonesia. Using 39 years of hydrometeorological data (1986–2024), including rainfall, reservoir inflow, and Oceanic Niño Index (ONI), the research identifies the climatic influence of El Niño–Southern Oscillation (ENSO) events on water availability and power generation sustainability. Results show a significant inverse correlation between ONI and both rainfall (r = –0.41) and inflow (r = –0.45), with El Niño years experiencing a 50–60% reduction in water inputs during dry months. La Niña events, in contrast, enhance inflow and precipitation, thereby supporting reservoir operations. Wavelet transform analysis reveals dominant periodicities in the 2–4 year range, consistent with ENSO cycles. These findings highlight the vulnerability of hydropower generation to climate variability and underscore the importance of adaptive reservoir management strategies based on ENSO projections. The study contributes to strategic planning in energy and water sectors, emphasizing the integration of climate forecasts in maintaining operational continuity of hydropower infrastructure.

To optimize the hydropower plant operations in the Sulawesi Generation Unit of PLN, this study proposes a data-driven approach to analyze electricity production by incorporating weather data. Utilizing historical data from January 2014 to December 2023, relevant indicators were extracted using machine learning algorithms. The integration of hydropower generation data, dam operational data, temperature, and rainfall enabled the prediction of electricity output through various models, including SARIMAX, Random Forest Regressor, Support Vector Regression, and Extreme Gradient Boosting. The dataset, consisting of 120 rows and 18 variables, demonstrated that combining diverse yet correlated data sources improve prediction accuracy. The best-performing model was validated and applied to forecast on new, unseen data. The findings indicate that machine learning offers a strategic advantage for PLN's decision-making in managing interconnected hydropower operations within the national power grid.

This study analyzes changes in rainfall, inflow discharge, and electricity production at PLTA Mrica using historical data (1985–2014) from CHIRPS (Climate Hazards Group InfraRed Precipitation with Station data) and six global climate models (GCMs) under CMIP6 (Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6). Future projections are based on the SSP5-8.5 (Shared Socioeconomic Pathway 5 – fossil-fueled development) scenario to represent a worst-case pathway, enabling assessment of maximum potential climate impacts on hydropower reliability [2] scenario for the period 2021–2100. A delta-based statistical downscaling method is applied to produce high-resolution rainfall projections. This method is deterministic in nature; it applies a fixed anomaly (delta) between future and historical climatologies onto observed datasets, without simulating transient atmospheric processes as done in prognostic models. It is computationally efficient and widely used for impact studies where capturing long-term mean changes is prioritized over day-to-day weather variability [2][3]. The results indicate an increase in rainfall during the wet season and a significant decline during the dry season, particularly from January to March, with projected rises of up to +2.5 mm/day, or approximately +30–40%, compared to the historical baseline. Conversely, the dry season (June–September) is projected to experience a decline of up to 1.5 mm/day, equivalent to a reduction of 25–40%, depending on the month and future time slice. Historical data indicate that monthly rainfall of at least 100–120 mm is generally required to sustain sufficient reservoir inflow for optimal electricity generation at PLTA Mrica, especially during the dry season. Variability in rainfall, particularly prolonged dry spells or delayed wet season onset, can lead to inflow shortages, reducing turbine operation hours and ultimately affecting annual energy output. This study highlights the importance of using climate data such as projected rainfall thresholds and variability to guide reservoir operations, optimize electricity production, and reduce risks during dry periods. Integrating such information supports more adaptive and resilient hydropower planning under future climate uncertainty.

The rapid global shift from fossil-based energy systems to renewable technologies has generated an urgent demand for frameworks that assess both environmental sustainability and economic feasibility. Life-Cycle Assessment (LCA) has emerged as a powerful tool to evaluate systematically the material inputs, energy use, emissions, and cost implications of renewable energy technologies across their entire life span—from raw material extraction and component fabrication to system operation, maintenance, and end-of-life management. This paper presents a systematic review and comparative analysis of four major renewable energy systems—solar photovoltaic (PV), wind, hydropower, and biomass—focusing on their life-cycle environmental impacts and economic performance. Results indicate that renewable energy technologies emit 70–90 percent fewer greenhouse gases compared to fossil-based systems, with solar PV and wind recording the lowest carbon footprints per unit of electricity produced. However, significant challenges persist, including high embodied energy in silicon purification for PV modules, turbine blade disposal in wind systems, ecological disturbances in hydropower, and extensive land-use requirements in biomass power generation. On the economic front, the levelized cost of energy (LCOE) for solar PV and onshore wind is increasingly competitive, in some cases achieving cost parity or falling below coal and natural gas, while hydropower remains viable in favorable geographies and biomass faces continued cost challenges due to complex supply chains. The study underscores that regional conditions, technological advancements, and effective end-of-life strategies strongly influence sustainability outcomes. The research directions to be implemented in the future involve the incorporation of circular economy practices, the use of digital twins as a predictive monitoring tool, and optimization using AI to improve environmental-economic analyses and make policy-related decisions.

Hydropower is left as one of the most stable and widely used forms of renewable energy sources such that it has been consuming a major share of the world electricity production but its efficacy, dependability and power quality is posing a challenge to its power conversion frameworks. Common two-level inverters have disadvantages in switching losses, being limited to medium and high-voltage operation, and both high harmonic distortion which can adversely affect grid stability and system life. Multilevel inverter (MLI) structures have been widely promising in this regard because they have the potential to generate near-sinusoidal waveforms with reduced Total Harmonic Distortion (THD), reduced electromagnetic interference and enhanced fault tolerance. In this paper, a comprehensive analysis of the major MLI topologies such as NPC, FC, CHB and MMC are presented and the applicability of these topologies to the small-, medium- and large- hydropower installations is discussed. It uses the full modeling and simulation, in MATLAB/Simulink and PSCAD, of a common hydropower generator connected to an 11 kV grid. The performance is experimented with parameters of harmonic distortion, switching and conduction losses, efficiency, fault withstanding and scalability to change of conditions in the operating hydropower. It is found that NPC and FC topologies have a moderate improvement and have their own limitations in terms of diode stress (NPC) and the problem of balancing capacitors (FC) respectively, thereby making them unfavorable candidates at large scale. Compared to it, the superior attributes of the CHB topology are its greater modularity and affordability of small to medium hydropower plants or efficiency levels above 96% with much reduced THD. In larger scale hydropower systems, MMC is the most versatile technology that in combination with its high efficiency ( >97%), low harmonic distortion ( <2%), scalability, modular redundancy is a very promising system. The results indicate that the multilevel inverters especially CHB and MMC are revolutionary technologies of hydropower due to the next generation hydropower plants and further improvements in performance, reliability, and sustainability are likely to be realized by adopting wide bandgap semiconductor devices, digital twin models, and AI-based predictive control right.

Increasing energy demand and reliance on fossil fuels is a driver for the exploration of alternative renewable energy sources, including hydropower generation. Sustainable micro-hydropower (MHP) energy installations can play an active role in decreasing this reliance on fossil fuels while decarbonising our electric grid, especially considering the more variable nature of other renewable sources. MHP coupled with the use of existing barriers in rivers can lower environmental impacts and costs of new micro-hydropower projects. However, the recently enacted nature restoration law (NRL) in Europe mandates for the removal or modification of a large number of existing river barriers to reconnect river ecosystems and enhance biodiversity.
